---
title: Configuration
---

This document describes the design of the configuration settings for the
Python classes and configuration files and tracks their implementation
status.

{{< include /docs/includes/_design-status.qmd >}}

## Overview

Data Packages range from simple (a few resources) to complex (many
resources with detailed schemas). Therefore, Flower's configuration lets
you customise output file types, content and structure (via templates),
and the output destination to fit different needs.

Configuration is split into two main levels:

- The top-level configuration dictates whether to use a built-in style
  or a custom style, the location of the template files for a custom
  style, and which sections to include (see
  [One and Many section classes](#one-and-many-class) for a definition
  of sections). This is represented by the `Config` class, the settings
  under the `[tool.seedcase-flower]` table in `pyproject.toml`, or the
  settings at the top level of the `.flower.toml` file. These
  configurations are only used by the `build` command and cannot be set
  on the CLI.
- The style-level configuration dictates which contents of the
  `datapackage.json` (**not individual properties**) are included in
  each section of the documentation and where those sections are
  outputted. This is represented by one or more `One` and `Many` section
  classes or `[[one]]` and `[[many]]` tables in the `sections.toml` file
  in the template directory and cannot be set in `pyproject.toml` or
  `.flower.toml`.

## Python classes

### {{< var done >}} `Config`

The `Config` class specifies the top-level configurations used by
`build` via three attributes: `style`, `template_dir`, and `output_dir`.
See the [Config](/docs/reference/Config.qmd) for details on each
attribute.

`output_dir` allows users to set the output location independently of
how a style structures its files internally. It defaults to `docs/`.

Flower uses [Jinja2](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/) to
generate documentation from `datapackage.json`. Because Jinja2 supports
any plain text output format (e.g., `.qmd` via `.qmd.jinja` templates),
output file types require no special handling when adding new built-in
styles.

### {{< var done >}} `One` and `Many` section classes {#one-and-many-class}

The main purpose of `One` and `Many` is to allow creating separate
"sections" of the documentation, in this case, separate files to display
different parts of the `datapackage.json` metadata. The `One` section
allows creating one output file but with potentially many `Content`
items inside, while the `Many` section creates many output files using a
single `Content`.

The `One` class has two attributes `output_path` and `contents`, where
multiple `Content` classes can be included in the `contents` list. The
`Many` class has almost the same attributes, except rather than having a
list of `Content` classes in `contents`, it includes the attributes of
the `Content` class in its own attributes. Because there are only a few
metadata properties that would benefit from using the `Many` section, we
decided to not allow the use of `jsonpath` and instead restrict `Many`
to `content` types of either `resources` or `fields` (for fields in a
resource's schema).

The `output_path` specifies the name of the output file or folder
relative to the `Config.output_dir`. `One.output_path` is a file path,
as it only outputs one file. `Many.output_path` will be used to create
many files. That's because some Data Package properties are arrays of
objects. For example, in the case of resources, we might want to create
a separate output file for each resource.

To expand on the `Many.output_path`, when a Data Package property that
we want to display is a list, like resources, we would set the output
path as a folder with the special `{}` whisker brackets in place of
where the file name should be to allow creating multiple files, one for
each resource. For now, we only allow properties that have a `name`
sub-property to output to multiple files. The reason we decided to use
the `name` property is that it has requirements in the Data Package
specification that make it ideal for use as a file name, specifically
that it can't have spaces and must be all lowercase.

For example, to create one output file per resource in a `resources/`
folder you would use the `output_path` and give it
`resources/{resource-name}.qmd`. You can also provide the folder as a
path like `resources/`, which would be equivalent to the above. Why
`resource-name` and not `name`? Because it allows for the creation of
multiple files and folders with custom names when multiple `name`
properties exist at different levels in a nested property. For example,
each schema field has a `name` property, as does the resource the fields
belong to. So to output a file for each schema field for each resource,
we use the `output_path` and give it
`resources/{resource-name}/fields/{resource-schema-field-name}.qmd`.

When setting a multi-file output, you can customise what properties get
sent to the Jinja2 template by using the `Section.contents` attribute.
See the section on the `Content` class below for more details.

See [`help(One)`](/docs/reference/One.qmd) or
[`help(Many)`](/docs/reference/Many.qmd) for more details.

### {{< var done >}} `Content`

The `Content` class provides a precise description of the path to the
Jinja2 template, which
[JSON Path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JSONPath) of the Data Package
property will be sent to the template, what the name of the Jinja2
variable is within the template, and whether the content represents one
or many files for properties that are arrays. We designed this class to
allow for flexibly creating complex custom documentation structures for
both the user and for us when we develop built-in styles.

See [`help(Content)`](/docs/reference/Content.qmd) for more details.

## Configuration file

<!-- TODO: Replace link with our own decision "why TOML" post -->

We use configuration files to ensure that how the documentation is built
is explicitly defined and reproducible whenever someone uses the
`seedcase-flower build` command. This way, anyone who has access to the
Data Package and the configuration file can re-build the documentation
in the same way with that simple command. We use TOML for the file
format since there are
[many advantages to it for storing configuration settings](https://www.anbowell.com/blog/an-in-depth-comparison-of-json-yaml-and-toml/),
especially in contrast to YAML. The two biggest advantages of TOML for
us are that you can use comments (with `#`) and that the content is
treated purely as data (whereas YAML can contain content that can be
parsed as code and executed).

The main configuration file maps one-to-one to the `Config` class
described above. The configuration can be put either in a separate
`.flower.toml` file or in the `pyproject.toml` file under the
`[tool.seedcase-flower]` table. The ordering of which configurations are
used is as follows:

1. If an argument is given to `style` in the `build` CLI command, use
   that.
2. If not, search for a `.flower.toml` file in the working directory
   and, if found, read the configurations within that file.
3. If `.flower.toml` does not exist, search for a `pyproject.toml` file
   in the working directory and, if found, read the configurations under
   the `[tool.seedcase-flower]` table.
4. If neither file exists, use the default configurations defined in the
   `Config` class, which represent the default built-in style.

The `sections.toml` configuration file kept within the template
directory (`Config.template_dir`) is used to create the style. This maps
directly to the `One`, `Many`, and `Content` classes. For any given
style, the template directory must have this `sections.toml` file, which
contains the settings for the `One` and `Many` classes. For built-in
styles, this `sections.toml` file is kept internally in Flower while for
custom styles, the user must provide it in their template directory.

To provide a clear precedence for applying settings, we decided that
styles specified on the CLI override settings in the configuration file.

### {{< var done >}} Main config settings: `.flower.toml`

The `.flower.toml` file contains the configuration settings for Flower.
For a simple configuration using a built-in style, the file can be as
simple as:

``` {.toml filename=".flower.toml"}
style = "quarto-one-page"
output-dir = "docs/"
```

Custom styles require `template-dir` to be included, for example:

``` toml
# The `templates-dir` below must include at least one Jinja and the
# `sections.toml` file.
template-dir = "path/to/templates/"
```

When `template-dir` is given, any value in `style` will be ignored.

### {{< var done >}} Main config settings: `pyproject.toml`

We allow the configuration settings to be set in the `pyproject.toml`
file under the `[tool.seedcase-flower]` table for convenience, which is
particularly useful if the Data Package is a Python project that uses
`pyproject.toml`. This way, no additional configuration file is needed
just for Flower.

Taking the complex example from `.flower.toml` above, the
`pyproject.toml` version would look like:

``` toml
[tool.seedcase-flower]
style = "custom"
template-dir = "templates/"
output-dir = "docs/"
```

### {{< var done >}} Main config settings: `sections.toml`

The `sections.toml` file contains the configuration settings for a given
style of output. The `sections.toml` is kept in the root of the
`Config.template_dir` and is used to create the `One` and `Many` section
classes and the `Content` classes within `One`. This file allows
creating a wide variety of styles, from simple to complex. For example:

``` toml
# This creates an `index.qmd` containing the combined `package` and `contributors`
# contents from the Jinja2 templates.
[[one]]
output-path = "index.qmd"
[[one.contents]]
jsonpath = "."
template-path = "path/to/templates/package.qmd.jinja"
jinja-variable = "package"
[[one.contents]]
jsonpath = ".contributors"
template-path = "path/to/templates/contributors.qmd.jinja"
jinja-variable = "contributors"

# This creates one file per resource in the `docs/resources/` folder.
# E.g. `docs/resources/demographics.qmd`, `docs/resources/blood.qmd`, etc.
[[many]]
output-path = "resources/"
# Or equivalently
# output-path = "resources/{resource-name}.qmd
content = "resources"
template-path = "path/to/templates/resource.qmd.jinja"
jinja-variable = "resource"

# This creates one YAML file for each field in a resource. The
# `{resource-name}` variable is replaced with the name of each resource and
# `{field-name}` is replaced with the name of each field. In this example, this
# would allow you to use custom Quarto listings for the
# fields: https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-listings.html#yaml-listing-content
[[many]]
output-path = "resources/{resource-name}/{field-name}.yml"
content = "fields"
template-path = "path/to/templates/resource-schema-field.yml.jinja"
jinja-variable = "field"
```
